title: Upcycling of cotton and cotton blend textile waste into functional nanofibrous membranes for enhanced oil sorption
content: The growing accumulation of textile waste has created an urgent need for effective strategies to convert discarded textiles into high-value functional materials. In this study, a versatile electrospinning strategy was developed to upcycle four cotton-containing textile feedstocks, including cotton nonwoven, post-consumer cotton shirt, cotton/polyester, and cotton/Lycra fabrics, into nanofibrous membranes for oil sorption applications. Notably, the cotton-blend textiles were processed without prior separation of their constituent fibers. Structural characterization revealed that the regeneration process transformed the original textile architectures into nanofibrous networks while retaining the characteristic chemical signatures of cellulose and the corresponding synthetic components. The resulting nanomembranes exhibited substantially enhanced oil sorption capacities compared with their original textile counterparts. Among the investigated materials, the cotton shirt-derived nanomembrane achieved the highest vacuum pump oil sorption capacity of 86.30 ± 3.30 g g−1, with sorption equilibrium reached within approximately 120 min. Furthermore, the cotton shirt-derived nanomembrane retained approximately 94% of its initial sorption capacity after five sorption–desorption cycles. These findings demonstrate the potential of electrospinning-based nanostructuring to valorize diverse cotton-containing textile wastes into reusable oil sorbents, providing a promising approach for textile waste upcycling and functional materials development.
